newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO, Israel tensions rise over Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: PLO, Israel tensions rise over Jerusalem.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians set themselves on a collision course over Jerusalem only days before the next deadline is reached in their interim peace accords.

The Palestinian Legislative Council called a general strike, a rare move since the Palestinian uprising ended with the signing of a framework peace accord in 1993, for Monday to protest at an Israeli building project in Arab East Jerusalem.

But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed that construction would go ahead, despite Palestinian opposition to the building of 6,500 homes for Jews on Jabal Abu Ghneim, a hill that Israel calls Har Homa.

Netanyahu, in a speech to his Likud party designed to silence right-wing critics who say he betrayed them by handing the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule in January, also had a warning for the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).

"If someone wants to declare, today, the establishment of a Palestinian state, let him do it. It will be a serious mistake, a severe mistake, that will bring a halt to the entire (peace) process," he said.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Saturday that he might declare a Palestinian state in reaction to the government's decision to approve the Jerusalem building project.
The next step in the Israeli-Palestinian peace process, mandated in the accord by which Israel handed 80 percent of Hebron to PLO rule, is a further Israeli withdrawal on the West Bank.

The pullback, the first of three in the Hebron accord timetable, should take place on March 7. Netanyahu's office said the government would meet on March 6 to discuss the scope of the withdrawal and vote on it.

Israel Channel One Television said in an unsourced report that Israel would hand over about five percent more of the West Bank to the PLO. It has already passed eight towns and some 400 villages to Palestinian rule.
Arafat, who is to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington on Monday, has tried to keep a lid on Palestinian rage over the Jerusalem building plan ahead of the next Israeli pullback.

He and Netanyahu both apparently fear a replay of last September's violence when 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in gun battles after Israel opened a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem.
Nonetheless tensions inched upwards in Hebron, long a flashpoint of Arab-Jewish violence and the only West Bank Palestinian town with Jewish settlers living in it.
Jews said vandals had smashed three gravestones in their cemetery early on Sunday and Palestinians said Jewish settlers roughed up Arab passers-by in the area late in the day.

Israel captured East Jerusalem along with the West Bank and the Gaza Strip in the 1967 Middle East war. In a move not recognised internationally, it later annexed East Jerusalem, declaring it part of an indivisible capital.

The Palestinians want to establish an independent state in the occupied territories with East Jerusalem as their capital. According to interim peace deals, the two sides are to reach a final peace accord in 1999.
